description: Take the Mysore Palace apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of the Amba Vilas Palace: the Wadiyar dynasty seat that burned at a wedding, rose again in Indo-Saracenic splendor, and became India's most visited palace after the Taj Mahal.

intro: Mysore's royal palace burned to the ground during a princess's wedding in 1897. Fifteen years later it reopened as Henry Irwin's Indo-Saracenic fantasy: 75 meters of grey granite, a 44-meter gold dome, and pink domes on every corner tower.
page_title: Mysore Palace: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: The Wadiyars had kept a palace on this ground since the 14th century, rebuilding it again and again across six hundred years. The wooden palace that stood here in 1897 caught fire during the wedding festivities of Princess Jayalakshmmanni and burned to the ground. Maharaja Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV and his mother, Maharani Kempananjammanni Devi, decided not to patch it up but to start over completely. They gave the commission to Henry Irwin, an English architect of the public works department, and told him to build the finest palace in India. Construction ran from 1897 to 1912 and cost Rs. 41.47 lakhs, a staggering sum for the time.
sections.heading: The palace that burned at a wedding

sections.body: Irwin designed in the Indo-Saracenic style, the British Raj's signature fusion of Islamic, Hindu, Rajput, Hoysala and Gothic elements. The result is three stories of grey granite about 75 meters long and 48 meters wide, with red granite accents, arched colonnades, bay windows and canopies. The defining feature is the five-story central tower, crowned by a gold-plated onion dome 44 meters above the ground. In a Rajasthani touch, the dome carries a small chhatri instead of a finial. At each of the cardinal points stands a square five-story tower topped with a pink dome. Above the large central archway of the main facade sits Gajalakshmi, the goddess of wealth flanked by elephants.
sections.heading: An English architect's Indian fantasy

sections.body: The palace works as a small walled city. Four gates pierce the grounds: Jaya Maarthaanda to the east, the main entrance; Jayarama to the north; Balarama to the south; and Varaha to the west. Bronze tigers sculpted by the British sculptor Robert William Colton flank the main approach. Inside, the Elephant Gate, or Ane Bagilu, a brass portal symbolizing power and strength, leads to the state rooms: the Public Durbar Hall where the Maharajas addressed their court, the Marriage Hall with its stained glass, the Doll's Pavilion. A Public Durbar Hall wing was added in the 1930s under Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar. After the Taj Mahal, it is the most visited attraction in India.
sections.heading: Gold, pink and granite

sections.body: Mysore Palace belongs to Dasara the way a stage belongs to its play. Every autumn the ten-day festival fills the city, and on Vijayadashami the palace is outlined in close to a hundred thousand light bulbs, glowing against the night while the royal elephant carries the golden howdah in procession. The Wadiyars ruled Mysore from 1399 to 1950, and the palace remains their official residence, managed today by the Government of Karnataka. The lights, the music and the crowds make it the rare monument that is still used the way it was built to be used: as the ceremonial heart of a kingdom.
sections.heading: The Dasara palace

sections.body:
The palace is so recognizable that filmmakers keep trying to get inside it, and keep being told no. In 2014 the crew of Rajinikanth's Lingaa asked permission to shoot a song at the Amba Vilas Palace and the palace officials refused outright, forcing the production to look elsewhere. Three years earlier Mani Ratnam had written to the authorities seeking permission to film key scenes of his planned Ponniyin Selvan adaptation at the palace during October and December 2011; that version of the film was never made, and the palace stayed out of it. The refusals have become part of the building's screen lore: the most filmed palace in South India is famous partly for the films that were not allowed in.

What the cameras do capture, every year without fail, is the Dasara illumination. The palace strung with nearly a hundred thousand bulbs is one of the most photographed sights in India, reproduced on postcards, tourism campaigns and news coverage of the festival each autumn. It ranks second only to the Taj Mahal among the country's most visited monuments, which makes its illuminated facade one of the most widely circulated architectural images in the world.
sections.heading: In the cultural conversation

timeline.text: The Wadiyars build the first palace on this ground; it is rebuilt repeatedly over six centuries.
The wooden palace burns down during the wedding of Princess Jayalakshmmanni.
Maharaja Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV and Maharani Kempananjammanni Devi commission Henry Irwin to rebuild; cost Rs. 41.47 lakhs.
The new Indo-Saracenic palace is completed.
The Public Durbar Hall wing is added under Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar.
Mani Ratnam seeks permission to film Ponniyin Selvan at the palace; the project is never made.
Palace officials refuse the Lingaa crew permission to shoot inside the palace.
